Thus in this wheel of existence, revolving like a chariot wheel, this host of beings meets another host of beings, each with its purpose.
mahabharata:12:9.33	There is happiness for one who abandons this worthless, endless cycle of existence, assailed by birth, death, old age, disease and pain.
mahabharata:12:9.34	When gods fall from heaven and great sages from their stations, who that knows the truth of cause would wish for any aim?
mahabharata:12:9.35	Having done various deeds of various marks, a king is bound by even slight causes through the earthly kings.
mahabharata:12:9.36	Therefore, this nectar of wisdom has long since come before me; having attained it, I seek the imperishable, eternal, steadfast station.
mahabharata:12:9.37	Living always by such a way of life, I shall support my body, following a fearless path.
[Bhima said:] "For one whose mind is set on idleness and who despises the duties of kings, what fruit is there in the destruction of the Dhritarashtras, bull of the Bharatas?
Forbearance, compassion, mercy and kindness do not exist for one following the kshatriya path, even toward a kinsman, in your view.
If we had known such a mind of yours, we would not have taken up weapons nor slain anyone.
We would have lived by begging until the release of the body, and this dreadful war of kings would not have been.
The wise know that all this is food for life; the moving and the unmoving are all the food of life.
The wise who know kshatriya dharma know that whoever obstructs a king who takes a kingdom must be slain.
Those obstructors of the kingdom, with their faults, have been slain by us; having slain them, enjoy this earth by dharma, Yudhishthira.
As a man who digs a well and, not reaching water, turns back smeared with mud, so is this deed of ours.
As a man who sets out on a long road with hope and, falling, turns back hopeless, so is this deed of ours.
As a man who, having slain his enemies, best of the Kurus, afterwards slays himself, so is this deed of ours.
As a hungry man who obtains food and does not eat it by chance, or a lover who, having won his beloved, does not enjoy her, so is this deed of ours.
We alone are to be blamed here, who of dull mind follow you, O king, thinking 'He is the eldest.'
We, strong in arm, learned and high-minded, stand by the word of a weakling as though powerless.
How would people not see us, the pathless, ruined, who have wasted our aims for the sake of a goal, as they see us now?
Renunciation is prescribed for a time of calamity, for one overcome by old age or afflicted by enemies.
Therefore the resolute here do not praise renunciation; the subtle-sighted consider this a transgression of dharma.
How could one born from it, devoted to it and resting on it, sit censuring it? Or is faith taken elsewhere?
The knowledge of Vedic doctrine promoted by the fortuneless, the penniless and unbelievers is a semblance of truth, an untruth.
It is possible to adopt shaven-headedness, supporting oneself by oneself, and to sit under a pretence of dharma, but not to live.
It is again possible to live happily alone in forests, not supporting sons, grandsons, gods, sages, guests and ancestors.
These deer, boars and birds are not conquerors of heaven; by this reckoning people do not call them meritorious.
If anyone obtained success by renunciation, O king, mountains and trees would quickly attain success.
These are seen to be ever renouncers, free of calamity, possessionless and always moving about in themselves.
But if one does not gain the success of others in one's own portion, then action alone must be done; there is no success without action.
Even water-born creatures attain success, who have only themselves to support and no other.
Consider how the world is engaged in its own various actions; therefore action alone is to be done; there is no success without action."
[Arjuna said:] "Some twice-born have left their homes and gone to the forest; fools, with beards not yet grown, born in families, they have gone forth.
Thinking 'This is dharma,' established in celibacy, abandoning homes and ancestors, Indra took pity on them.
The revered one, becoming a golden bird, spoke to them: 'What those who eat the remnants (of sacrifice) have done is hard for men to do.
Their deed is meritorious and their life praiseworthy; they are perfected and have gained the foremost state, devoted to dharma.'
[The sages said:] 'Ah, this bird praises the remnant-eaters; surely it instructs us, and we are remnant-eaters.'
[The bird said:] 'I do not praise you, smeared with mud, dusty, eaters of leavings, fools; others are the remnant-eaters.'
[The sages said:] 'We worship this as the highest good; tell us, bird, what is the good; we greatly trust you.'
[The bird said:] 'If you do not distrust me, and separate yourselves by yourselves, then I shall tell you the truth, beneficial words.'
[The bird said:] 'Among quadrupeds the cow is best; among metals gold is best; among sounds the mantra is best; among bipeds the Brahmana is best.
For a Brahmana the mantra-rites of birth and so on are ordained, up to the funeral at the cremation ground, at the proper time while he lives.
His Vedic rites are the unsurpassed road to heaven; all rites are said to be perfected by mantras.
Success is desired here by those firm in the traditions; the months, half-months, seasons, sun, moon and stars,
all beings strive; that is the truth for those attached to rites; this is the holy field of success, this the great stage of life.
But men who censure rites and have gone astray, fools without wealth, have sin.
Fools who, abandoning the eternal lines of the gods, ancestors and Brahma, act so, go thereafter to the path of the unheard.
Let this be your austerity, joined to giving, as urged by the sages; therefore austerity is said to be what one resolves upon.
Dividing the eternal lines of gods, ancestors and Brahma, and serving the teacher—that is called hard.
The gods, having done what is hard, reached supreme glory; therefore I tell you that carrying the householder's life is hard.
Austerity is the best, the root of creatures, without doubt, by this rule of family life, in which everything is established.
The Brahmanas, beyond dualities and free of envy, know this as austerity; therefore the forest and the middle are called austerity in the worlds.
The remnant-eaters go to an unassailable state: those who, dividing food at evening and morning in their own family according to rule,
and giving to guests, gods, ancestors and their own people, eat what is left, they call remnant-eaters.
Therefore, resorting to their own dharma, of good vows, truth-speaking, becoming teachers of the world, they become unblemished.
Reaching heaven in Shakra's world, free of envy, those who do the hard deed dwell for eternal years.'
Then, hearing that word of his, joined to dharma and wealth, they gave up the path of unbelief and took to the householder's dharma.
Therefore you too, invincible one, taking up eternal steadfastness, rule the whole earth, your enemies slain, best of men."
[Vaishampayana said:] Humouring his brother's mind, the wide-chested, mighty-armed, copper-faced, measured-speaking subduer of foes (Nakula) spoke.

The fires on the sacrificial posts of all the gods are piled up; therefore know, great king, that the gods stand on the path of action.
mahabharata:12:12.4	Those who are givers of life to the believers, and the ancestors, too perform only action; behold the rule, O king; and those who are cast out by the Vedic doctrine, know them to be utter unbelievers.
mahabharata:12:12.5	A Brahmana, abandoning what the Veda declares in all rites, does not reach the heights of heaven by the path of the gods, Bharata.
mahabharata:12:12.6	'This goes beyond all stages of life,' say the Vedic conclusions, Brahmanas versed in the scriptures; know them, lord of men.
mahabharata:12:12.7	He who spends wealth gained by dharma in the chief sacrifices, great king, among the self-controlled, is called the true renouncer.
mahabharata:12:12.8	One who gives up himself without regard to taking pleasure, and is established above, great king, is a renouncer of the tamasic sort, lord.
mahabharata:12:12.9	The homeless wanderer, the sage dwelling at a tree's root, never cooking, ever in yoga, is a renouncer, Partha, a mendicant.
mahabharata:12:12.11	The wise say the stages of life have been weighed on a balance: on one side the three, O king, and on the other the householder's stage.
mahabharata:12:12.12	He who looks to the aim of wealth, desire and heaven, Bharata—this is the path of the great sages, this the course of those who know the world.
mahabharata:12:12.13	He who holds this view is a renouncer, bull of the Bharatas, not he who, abandoning his home, goes to the forest like a fool.
mahabharata:12:12.14	When the dishonest man who uses dharma as a decoration looks to desires, Death, the king, binds him by the noose of death at the throat.
mahabharata:12:12.15	A deed done from pride is not called fruitful; all that is joined to renunciation, great king, bears great fruit.
mahabharata:12:12.16	Peace, self-control, austerity, giving, truth, purity, uprightness, sacrifice, steadfastness and dharma are ever the rule of the sages.
mahabharata:12:12.17	Undertaking rites for ancestors, gods and guests is praised here; and here alone, great king, the triple aim is the whole fruit.
mahabharata:12:12.18	For the renouncer who abides in this rule practised by Brahmanas, there is never any loss of what has been done.
mahabharata:12:12.19	The sinless Prajapati created beings, O king, with a tranquil soul, thinking 'They will sacrifice to me with sacrifices of various fees.'
mahabharata:12:12.20	Creepers and trees, and herbs for sacrifice, pure animals, and oblations for sacrifice were made.
mahabharata:12:12.21	That sacrificial work of the householder in his stage is not at variance; therefore the householder's life is hard and rare here.
mahabharata:12:12.22	Householders who have attained it, with cattle and grain, and do not sacrifice, great king, have eternal sin in them.
mahabharata:12:12.23	Some sages spread their sacrifices of Vedic study, others sacrifices of knowledge, and others the great sacrifices by mind alone.
mahabharata:12:12.24	For one who follows the path of giving and concentration, O king, a twice-born who has become Brahma, the dwellers in heaven long.
mahabharata:12:12.25	You speak of unbelief without ever having given up in sacrifices the wondrous jewels gathered from here and there; I see no renunciation in one who keeps a family, lord of men.
mahabharata:12:12.26	Sacrifice, great king, with the Rajasuya, Ashvamedha and Sarvamedha, and other sacrifices honoured by Brahmanas, dear one, as Shakra, lord of the gods, did.
mahabharata:12:12.27	A king who, by his negligence, lets his subjects be plundered by robbers, and gives them no refuge, is called Kali (the evil age) as king.
mahabharata:12:12.28	Horses, cows, female slaves, female elephants, well adorned, villages and countries, fields and houses,
mahabharata:12:12.29	without giving them to the twice-born, with minds filled with envy, we, lord of men, will become the evil of kings.
mahabharata:12:12.30	Non-givers, without refuge, sharers in the sin of kings, they enjoy sorrows only, never happiness.
mahabharata:12:12.31	If, without having sacrificed with great sacrifices, without having made the ancestral offering, you go forth without giving up at the tirthas,
mahabharata:12:12.32	you will go to ruin like a torn cloud driven by the wind, fallen from both worlds and standing in between.
mahabharata:12:12.33	One would be a renouncer by abandoning whatever within or without causes distraction of mind, not he who stands having merely left.
mahabharata:12:12.34	For a Brahmana abiding in this rule practised by Brahmanas, great king, there is never any loss.
mahabharata:12:12.35	Having forcibly slain the prosperous enemies as Shakra slew the Daitya hosts in battle, who, Partha, intent on his own dharma, would grieve, O king, following what was remembered by the ancients and practised by the good?
mahabharata:12:12.36	Having conquered the earth by kshatriya dharma and valour and given it to those who know the mantras, you will go to the heights of heaven, king; you ought not to grieve now, Partha.
[Sahadeva said:] "For one freed from outward possessions yet greedy for bodies, whatever dharma or happiness there is, let that be so for our enemies.
For one who has given up bodily possessions yet rules the earth, whatever dharma or happiness there is, let that be so for our friends.
Death is of two syllables, Brahma of three, eternal; 'mine' is death, 'not mine' is eternal.
Brahma and Death, O king, both rest in the self; unseen, they surely make beings fight.
If, Bharata, this being's imperishability is fixed, then splitting the bodies of beings will not be violence.
Or if the origin and dissolution of being are joined, then with the body destroyed all would be destroyed and the path of action would be in vain.
Therefore, abandoning the extreme, one who knows should follow the path practised by the good of former and still more ancient times.
The king who, having won the whole earth with its moving and unmoving things, does not enjoy it rightly, has a fruitless life.
Or if, O king, he dwells in the forest living on wild produce, but has possessiveness toward his goods, he is in the mouth of Death.
See, Bharata, the nature of beings outward and inward; those who see that nature are freed from great fear.
You are my father, you my mother, you my brother, you my teacher; therefore forgive me, afflicted, for my lamentation of grief.
Whether true or untrue, what I have said, know it, protector of the earth, to be from devotion, best of the Bharatas."
[Vaishampayana said:] Of great family, glorious, long-eyed, the best of women, Draupadi, spoke to the king of kings.
To the bull among kings, seated surrounded by his brothers like a lord of the herd by elephants like lions and tigers,
she, ever proud, especially toward Yudhishthira, ever cherished by the king, knowing dharma and seeing dharma,
the broad-hipped one, addressing him in a most sweet, gentle voice, looking at her husband, then spoke these words:

These brothers of yours, Partha, stand drying up like chataka birds, crying out, and you do not gladden them.
mahabharata:12:14.7	Gladden them, great king, like rutting great elephants, always sharers of your sorrow, with fitting speech.
mahabharata:12:14.8	How, king, in Dvaitavana earlier, did you say these words to these brothers together, afflicted by cold, wind and heat:
mahabharata:12:14.9	'Having slain Duryodhana in battle, we shall enjoy the earth, replete with all desires, eager for victory in the fight,
mahabharata:12:14.11	sacrificing with various abundant sacrifices with proper fees, the sorrow of our forest dwelling will become happiness for us.'
mahabharata:12:14.12	Having said this to them yourself, best of upholders of dharma, how do you today, hero, again break their hearts?
mahabharata:12:14.13	A weakling does not enjoy the earth, a weakling does not gain wealth, and a weakling's sons in his house sit like fish in mud.
mahabharata:12:14.14	A kshatriya without the rod does not shine; one without the rod does not gain prosperity; subjects of a king without the rod do not prosper in happiness, Bharata.
mahabharata:12:14.15	Friendliness to all beings, giving, study and austerity are the dharma of a Brahmana, not of a king, best of kings.
mahabharata:12:14.16	Restraining the wicked and protecting the good, and not fleeing from battle—this is the highest dharma of kings.
mahabharata:12:14.17	He in whom are forbearance and anger, giving and taking, fear and fearlessness, restraint and favour, is called a knower of dharma.
mahabharata:12:14.18	Not by learning, nor by giving, nor by conciliation, nor by sacrifice, nor even by bribery was this earth won by you.
mahabharata:12:14.19	That army of the enemies, raised up, hero, with elephants, horses and chariots, greater with its three arms,
mahabharata:12:14.20	guarded by Drona and Karna, Ashvatthaman and Kripa—that was slain by you, hero; therefore enjoy the earth.
mahabharata:12:14.21	Jambudvipa, great king, with its tens of thousands of countries, was crushed by you with the rod, tiger among men.
mahabharata:12:14.22	Krauncha-dvipa, like Jambudvipa, king, to the west of great Meru, was crushed by you with the rod.
mahabharata:12:14.23	Shaka-dvipa, like Krauncha-dvipa, to the east of great Meru, was crushed by you with the rod.
mahabharata:12:14.24	Bhadrashva, to the north of great Meru, measured like Shaka-dvipa, was crushed by you with the rod, tiger among men.
mahabharata:12:14.25	The islands with their intermediate islands, the abodes of various peoples, plunging into the ocean, hero, were crushed by you with the rod.
mahabharata:12:14.26	Having done these incomparable deeds, Bharata, you are not pleased, great king, though honoured by the twice-born.
mahabharata:12:14.27	Behold these brothers, Bharata, and be glad, like bulls in rut, like mighty lords of elephants.
mahabharata:12:14.28	All are like immortals, scorchers of foes, able to bear enemies; I think even one of them could bring happiness.
mahabharata:12:14.29	How much more my husbands, bulls among men, tigers among men, like all the senses in the body's activity.
mahabharata:12:14.30	My mother-in-law, omniscient and all-seeing, did not speak falsely: 'Yudhishthira will place you, Panchali, in the supreme happiness.'
mahabharata:12:14.31	Having quickly with valour slain many thousands of kings, I see that as vain through your delusion, O lord of men.
mahabharata:12:14.32	Those whose eldest is mad, all of them serve him; by your madness, king of kings, all the Pandavas are mad.
mahabharata:12:14.33	If your brothers were not mad, O lord of men, they would bind you and rule the earth together with the unbelievers.
mahabharata:12:14.34	One who is thus foolish and does not attain the good is to be treated with fumigations, ointments, rites and medicines—he who goes the wrong way.
mahabharata:12:14.35	I am the lowest of all women in the world, bull of the Bharatas, I who, so wronged by enemies, wish to live.
mahabharata:12:14.36	From these who strive, prosperity arises; but you, having won the whole earth, bring calamity on yourself.
mahabharata:12:14.37	As Mandhata and Ambarisha were the two best kings of the earth, esteemed by kings, so you shine, O king.
mahabharata:12:14.38	Rule the goddess earth, protecting the subjects by dharma, with her mountains, forests and islands; do not be downcast, O king.
mahabharata:12:14.39	Sacrifice with various sacrifices, offering to the fires, and give cities, enjoyments and garments to the twice-born, best of kings.
[Arjuna said:] "The rod governs all subjects; the rod alone protects; the rod is awake among the sleeping; the wise know the rod as dharma.
The rod protects dharma, lord of men, and likewise wealth; the rod protects desire; the triple aim is called the rod.
By the rod grain is protected, by the rod wealth is protected; learned one, take this, see the worldly nature.
Some sinners do not sin from fear of the king's rod, some from fear of Yama's rod, some from fear of the next world,
some from fear of one another; thus in the world as constituted, everything rests on the rod.
From fear of the rod alone some do not eat one another; they would sink in blind darkness if the rod did not guard.
Because it tames the untamed and punishes the ill-behaved, the wise know it as the rod (danda) from taming and punishing.
For Brahmanas the rod is in speech, for kshatriyas the offering of the arm; for the Vaishya the rod is said to be giving, and the Shudra is said to be without the rod.
Where the dark, red-eyed rod moves, truthful, the subjects are not bewildered, if the leader sees rightly.
The celibate student, the householder, the forest-dweller and the mendicant stay on their path only from fear of the rod.
No one unafraid sacrifices, O king; no one unafraid wishes to give; no man unafraid wishes to stay within the agreement.
Without cutting vital parts, without a cruel deed, without slaying like a fisherman, one does not gain great fortune.
There is no fame here for one who does not slay, nor wealth, nor offspring; Indra became Mahendra only by slaying Vritra.
The very gods who are slayers are greatly honoured by the world: Rudra, Skanda, Shakra, Fire, Varuna, Yama,
Time the slayer, Wind, Death, Vaishravana, the Sun, the Vasus, Maruts, Sadhyas and Vishvedevas, Bharata.
People bow to these gods in submission, mighty one; never to Brahma, Dhata or Pushan.
Some tranquil men in all rites worship the impartial, self-controlled, peace-devoted.
I do not see anyone in the world living by non-violence; beings live on beings, the strong on the weak.
The mongoose eats mice, the cat the mongoose, the dog eats the cat, O king, and the wild beast the dog.
Man eats them all; see how dharma came about; all this moving and unmoving is the food of life.
The ordinance made by the gods—the wise man is not bewildered by it; as you were created, O king of kings, so should you be.
Forest-dwelling fools who have restrained anger and joy do not support life without killing, ascetics though they be.
In water are many creatures, on earth and in fruits; no one fails to kill them, what else for sustaining life?
There are subtle beings known only by inference, for whom by the falling of an eyelash the course of life is altered.
Sages who have left villages, free of anger and envy, are seen bewildered in the forest, keeping family dharma.
Men splitting the earth, cutting herbs, trees, egg-born creatures and animals, perform sacrifices, and they attain heaven.
When the science of the rod is established, all undertakings succeed, son of Kunti, for all beings; of this I have no doubt.
If the rod did not exist in the world, these subjects would perish; the strong would roast the weak on a spit like fish.
This truth was spoken earlier by Brahma: the rod, rightly applied, protects the subjects; see the fires: unafraid they are quenched, but threatened, they blaze for fear of the rod."
Knowing this, how do you consider me guilty as the serpent? And if it is so, you also are guilty.
Having myself destroyed the earth, best of the twice-born, how can I levy tax for the sacrifice from those given to grief?
Likewise Bhimasena too could not bear King Dhritarashtra, O king of kings, and always was displeased in heart.
The horses took away the divine chariot, sun-coloured, yoked, in the sight of Daruka, and the four best horses, swift as thought, moved above the sea.
When that hero, fair-looking Nakula, had fallen, Bhima then again said this to the king:
Hearing the words of the king of dharma, he turned back; and the divine messenger said to him, "This is as far as you were to go."
